title: Name origins
subtitle: Where words come from
about: Where everyday words, scientific terms, months and eponyms really come from, checked against etymological dictionaries. Famous false etymologies are included, answered with the truth.

cards.note: Ariadne gave Theseus a clew of thread so he could find his way back out of the Minotaur's labyrinth.
In the 1200s it meant 'foolish'; it drifted through 'fussy' and 'precise' before meaning 'agreeable' by 1769.

cards.answer: Latin com + panis, 'one who shares bread'
cards.note: Probably a translation of a Germanic word: Gothic gahlaiba, 'messmate', was likewise built on hlaib, 'loaf'.
An astrological word: a calamity was blamed on the unfavourable position of a star or planet at the time.
Originally an unglazed hole in the roof; it replaced the Old English word eagþyrl, literally 'eye-hole'.
Its German cousin selig still means 'blessed'; in English it slid from 'innocent' to 'pitiable' to 'foolish'.
The deal dies either way: when the debt is repaid, or when payment fails and the land is lost.
Walter Scott popularised it in 1822 but wrongly read it as 'bare shirt', a warrior fighting without armour.

cards.answer: Old English mare, a goblin that smothers sleepers
cards.note: Nothing to do with horses: the mare was an evil spirit believed to cause a feeling of suffocation in sleep.

cards.answer: Persian shāh māt, 'the king is helpless'
cards.note: Arabic speakers took it as 'the king is dead'; check and chess come from the same royal word, shāh.
A medieval evening bell told households to cover or bank their hearths, so untended fires would not spread overnight.
Sixteenth century spellings include 'God be wy you' and 'God buy'; greetings like 'good day' turned God into good.
The story that Roman soldiers were paid in salt is unproven; salarium may have been an allowance for buying salt.
A flexing biceps was thought to look like a mouse moving under the skin; Greek mys also means both.
Named for the tiny image of yourself you see reflected in another person's eye; Greek korē meant both 'girl' and 'pupil'.
The fever was blamed on foul air from marshes; it is now known to be spread by mosquitoes, which breed there.
English borrowed it during a 1743 epidemic that began in Italy, where disease had long been blamed on astral influence.
Ragusa, now Dubrovnik, first isolated arrivals for thirty days in 1377 against the Black Death; forty days followed later.
Hippocrates and Galen likened some tumours, with their swollen surrounding veins, to crabs; Greek karkinos also meant both.
Named because the pain often strikes one side of the head; the older English form megrim also meant low spirits.
Black bile was one of the four humours of ancient medicine; an excess of it was blamed for gloom and sadness.
First the name of a chant in the vespers for the dead; by 1785 it meant a medicine given to please, not cure.
In 1587 the anatomist Aranzi likened this curved ridge in the brain first to a silkworm, then to a seahorse.
Named for the copious urine passing through the body; the same Greek word also meant a drawing compass, legs astride.

cards.answer: Gell-Mann's coinage, spelled from Joyce's Finnegans Wake
cards.note: Gell-Mann had the sound 'kwork' in mind first, then found 'Three quarks for Muster Mark' in James Joyce's novel.
Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R. made the word famous, but Karel credited his brother Josef with suggesting it.

cards.answer: Greek khaos, 'chaos', respelled by van Helmont
cards.note: The Flemish chemist wrote that he called this unknown vapour 'by a new name, gas'; Dutch g sounds like Greek kh.

cards.answer: Acronym: light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation
cards.note: Modelled on maser, in which the m stood for microwave; Gordon Gould first published the acronym LASER in 1959.
Gilbert coined electricus, 'like amber', in 1600 for rubbed amber's pull; Stoney named the electron in 1891.
For centuries it meant only our Milky Way; other galaxies were confirmed as separate star systems in the 1920s.
Jenner protected people from smallpox using cowpox; in 1881 Pasteur extended the term to all such inoculations, honouring Jenner.
They wandered against the fixed stars; the ancient planets included the Sun and Moon but not the Earth.
Its glowing tail looked like streaming hair; comets were long feared as omens of plague and the fall of kingdoms.
Leucippus and Democritus imagined indivisible particles; John Dalton revived the word in 1805, long before physicists split atoms.

cards.answer: Coined by William Whewell, by analogy with artist
cards.note: Whewell wanted a name for 'a cultivator of science in general' and coined physicist in the same work.
Edoardo Amaldi coined it as a joke to distinguish it from Chadwick's heavy neutron; Enrico Fermi made it standard.
Kepler applied it to Jupiter's moons in the 1610s; Galileo, who discovered them, had named them after the Medici.
Richard Owen coined it in the early 1840s; by deinos he meant 'fearfully great', evoking size and majesty.
From the title of al-Khwarizmi's ninth-century treatise on equations; in early English algebra could also mean bone-setting.
Cipher comes from the same Arabic word; it shifted from 'zero' to 'any numeral' to 'secret code'.

cards.answer: Nahuatl āhuacatl, 'avocado'; 'testicle' was only a euphemism
cards.note: Spanish reshaped aguacate into avocado, 'lawyer', by folk etymology; English speakers turned it into 'alligator pear'.
Probably a translation of medieval Latin aqua vitae; French eau de vie, used for brandy, means the same.

cards.answer: Probably Hokkien kê-chiap, 'brine of pickled fish'
cards.note: Early English ketchups were made from mushrooms, oysters, mussels or walnuts; tomato became the standard much later.

cards.answer: Italian, after the brown habits of Capuchin friars
cards.note: Viennese coffee houses of the late 1700s served a Kapuziner: coffee with a few drops of cream, matching the robes.
The tropical fruit took the name in the 1660s for its cone-like look; 'pine cone' then replaced the original meaning.

cards.answer: Spanish vainilla, 'little pod', from Latin vagina, 'sheath'
cards.note: Named for the shape of its long seed pods; Cortés's soldiers encountered vanilla in Mexico around 1521.
It began as a quince paste; marmelo goes back to Greek melimēlon, 'honey apple'. Citrus versions came in the 1600s.
Named for the milky sap of its cut stem; lac shares an ancient root with Greek gala, the source of galaxy.
Italian biscotti keep the original twice-baked idea; in American English a biscuit became a soft bun by 1818.
Romans seasoned raw vegetables with brine; salad, salary and sauce all go back to Latin sal, 'salt'.

cards.answer: Arabic al-kuhl, 'kohl', a fine eye powder
cards.note: It first meant any fine powder; Paracelsus also used it for a volatile liquid, and 'spirit of wine' followed.

cards.answer: Janus, Roman god of doorways and beginnings
cards.note: Janus was shown with two faces looking in opposite directions; his name meant 'gate' or 'arched passageway'.
Named for a Roman feast of purification held mid-month; it was long the last month of the Roman year, which began in March.

cards.answer: Uncertain; perhaps Etruscan Apru, from Aphrodite
cards.note: The old story linking it to Latin aperire, 'to open', like spring buds, is a folk etymology without support.

cards.answer: Julius Caesar, born in that month
cards.note: Renamed in his honour after his death; before that the Romans called it Quintilis, the 'fifth' month.
Renamed from Sextilis, 'sixth', in 8 BCE; later emperors tried renaming other months too, but those names never stuck.
The early Roman year began in March, so September to December were months seven to ten, as their names say.

cards.answer: Old English mōnandæg, 'day of the moon'
cards.note: A translation of Latin Lunae dies, which also gives French lundi and Spanish lunes; Greek used the same idea.
Tiw stood in for Mars, as in French mardi; his name comes from the same ancient root as Zeus.
Woden, Norse Odin, was matched with Mercury, as in French mercredi; German simply says Mittwoch, 'midweek'.
Thor was matched with Jupiter, as in French jeudi; German Donnerstag means plainly 'thunder day'.

cards.answer: Frigg, Germanic goddess of married love
cards.note: Frigg stood in for Venus, as in French vendredi; some Icelandic writers preferred Freyja, a closer match to Venus.

cards.answer: Saturn, Roman god of the planet
cards.note: The only English weekday to keep its Roman god; Swedish lördag and Danish lørdag mean 'bath day'.

cards.answer: Captain Charles Boycott, an Irish land agent, 1880
cards.note: The Irish Land League isolated him in County Mayo in 1880; newspapers across Europe soon borrowed his name for the tactic.

cards.answer: Dr Joseph-Ignace Guillotin, who urged humane beheading
cards.note: He neither invented the machine nor wanted executions: he opposed the death penalty. Physician Antoine Louis designed the prototype.

cards.answer: General Ambrose Burnside, with 'burnsides' flipped around
cards.note: The Union Civil War general wore bushy side whiskers with a shaven chin; burnsides became sideburns by 1880.

cards.answer: Étienne de Silhouette, French finance minister, 1759
cards.note: The usual explanation: anything skimpy or austere was mocked as 'à la Silhouette', after his unpopular economies.
A popular story says he ate meat between slices of bread so he could stay at the gaming table; Cook named islands after him.

cards.answer: Samuel Maverick, a Texan rancher who left calves unbranded
cards.note: Unbranded strays were called mavericks; the sense 'independent thinker' grew popular through his grandson, congressman Maury Maverick.
His name means 'native of Khwarazm'; the spelling was later reshaped by mistaken association with Greek arithmos, 'number'.
In experiments published in 1791 he made dead frogs' legs twitch with electricity; coating iron with zinc took the name in 1839.
From 1778 Mesmer promoted 'animal magnetism' in Paris, claiming an invisible fluid let one person influence another.

cards.answer: Jean Nicot, French ambassador to Portugal
cards.note: In 1561 he sent tobacco seeds and powdered leaves from Lisbon to France; the tobacco genus Nicotiana honours him.
Volta's pile of 1799, stacked zinc and copper discs separated by brine, was the first battery to give steady current.
The acronym story appears only by 1933 with no evidence; slang posh for 'money' or 'a dandy' came earlier.

cards.answer: Probably Middle Dutch colf, 'club'; not an acronym
cards.note: Recorded in a Scottish statute of 1457 banning golf and football; the acronym story seems to date only from 1997.

cards.answer: Latin sincerus, 'pure, whole'; not sine cera, 'without wax'
cards.note: The tale of honest sculptors using no wax to hide flaws is dismissed by the OED; the real root is uncertain.

cards.answer: Plural of 'new', after French nouvelles; not compass points
cards.note: The north, east, west, south joke is recorded by 1640, mostly in jest-books; it was never a serious derivation.

cards.answer: Chosen for easy Morse; not 'save our souls'
cards.note: Three dots, three dashes, three dots are sent unbroken; it is simple to send and hard to mistake.

cards.answer: French surlonge, 'above the loin'; never knighted
cards.note: Tales of a king knighting the beef as 'Sir Loin' date from 1655; the word was in use long before.

cards.answer: DuPont coinage, perhaps from 'no-run'; not New York plus London
cards.note: DuPont said the name went no-run, nuron, nilon, nylon, since stockings were not truly run-proof. London was never involved.

cards.answer: 'Oll korrect', an 1839 joke spelling of all correct
cards.note: One of many jokey abbreviations in 1830s America; Martin Van Buren's 'Old Kinderhook' campaign of 1840 spread it.

cards.answer: Hawaiian wiki, 'quick'; not 'what I know is'
cards.note: Ward Cunningham named his 1995 website after the Wiki Wiki Shuttle bus at Honolulu airport, wanting to avoid 'quick-web'.

cards.answer: Engineers' slang by the 1870s; not Hopper's 1947 moth
cards.note: Thomas Edison wrote of 'bugs' in inventions in 1878; the moth taped into a Harvard computer log came much later.
